input: I'm a master's student with one GPU. Why do language models still make things up, and what's still hard about catching it?
verdict: A busy field, picked so labs would agree: hallucination. 80 papers, 75 in full, 232 of 250 quotes kept (93%), 81 s. Strong cited answer; two first steps link the papers' own code. But all six problems came from one group each and no group spanned papers, though four labs wrote that factuality is judged by LLM judges for lack of human labels. Not saved as an example. A recruit step was built and tested on its quotes: one clean two-lab problem (grounding needs a complete knowledge base).
search: Searching arXiv for “hallucination detection language models”, “hallucination”, “factuality”, “faithfulness”
field: truthfulness and hallucination detection in language models

terms.meaning: when a language model generates text that sounds plausible but is factually incorrect or unsupported by input
the degree to which a model's output aligns with verifiable facts or known knowledge
whether a model's output stays true to the information provided in its input or context
how well a model's responses are anchored in reliable sources or evidence rather than invented content
methods used to identify when a model's output contains hallucinations or factual errors
processes that check model outputs against external knowledge bases or trusted sources to confirm accuracy

sentences.text: Language models still make things up because standard alignment methods like RLHF optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality, and factuality-specific alignment methods have not reproduced independently or beaten base models on common benchmarks [2610.18415].

A core reason detection stays hard is that widely used faithfulness metrics measure only precision, whether stated claims are supported, and ignore recall, so a model that says almost nothing can score near-perfect faithfulness while missing most relevant facts [2606.09376].

Token-level detectors fail exactly when the generating model is confidently wrong, and low-false-alarm onset detection has a fundamental delay bound of roughly 1.3 tokens even under ideal conditions, with real detectors catching under a third of onsets at that budget [2608.18115, 2606.12476].

Evaluation itself is fragile because benchmarks often lack ground truth for prompts, forcing reliance on LLM judges and retrieval that can be systematically biased relative to human judgments [2610.18415, 2609.00494].

read_first.why: Shows why alignment doesn't fix factuality and why evaluation is fragile
Explains the precision-recall blind spot in faithfulness metrics
Details why token-level detection fails on confident errors
Quantifies fundamental delay bounds for onset detection
Describes human-anchored evaluation to fix judge bias

problems.title: Hallucination detection struggles with multi-hop reasoning

statements.quote: Rare but complex cases, for example, failures in multi-hop reasoning across multiple pieces of evidence, may still occur and may not be captured by FSA.
statements.label: uncaptured complex failure modes like multi-hop reasoning

problems.explanation: Current hallucination detectors miss errors that require chaining together several pieces of evidence, known as multi-hop reasoning failures. The paper shows that even with strategic human annotation, these rare but complex cases can slip through the FSA method.
problems.first_step: Reproduce the strategic annotation sampling from "Human-Anchored Factuality Evaluation with Strategic Annotation" on a small public QA dataset such as HotpotQA. Use an LLM judge to score all examples, then apply the paper's selective sampling to choose a subset for human labeling, and measure whether the human-annotated subset catches more multi-hop errors than random sampling.

problems.title: Confidence scores don't reliably indicate truthfulness

statements.quote: self-reported confidence is poorly aligned with factual truthfulness
statements.label: confidence scores do not reliably indicate truthfulness

problems.explanation: Models often report high confidence when they are factually wrong, so self-reported confidence cannot be trusted as a truthfulness signal. The OpenHalDet benchmark was built to test detectors across many generation settings, giving a common ground to study this misalignment. A reliable confidence, truthfulness link would let systems flag uncertain outputs without extra labeling cost.
problems.first_step: Clone the OpenHalDet repository from https://github.com/Nellie179/Hallucination-Detection and run the provided evaluation scripts on the benchmark's included generation scenarios. Compare each detector's confidence scores against the ground-truth factuality labels to quantify the alignment gap.

problems.title: Token-level AUC overestimates performance due to dependence assumption

statements.quote: Token-level AUC treats tokens within the same example as independent observations, which inflates effective sample size; example-level AUC (0.795 for BiGRU) is consistently lower but preserves model rankings.
statements.label: token-level AUC overestimates performance due to dependence assumption

problems.explanation: Token-level AUC treats every token as an independent data point, which artificially inflates the effective sample size and makes detectors look better than they are. The paper shows that example-level AUC is consistently lower but preserves model rankings, so switching to example-level metrics gives a truer picture of detection quality.
problems.first_step: Using the code from "Temporal Multi-Signal Fusion for Token-Level Hallucination Detection" at https://github.com/YehudaItkin/temporal-hallucination-detection, run the BiGRU detector on its test set and compute both token-level and example-level AUC. Report the gap between the two metrics to confirm the inflation effect.

problems.title: Lack of suitable datasets for non-entity-centric text hallucination evaluation

statements.quote: Extending the evaluation to less entity-centric long-form generations remains challenging because few datasets provide fine-grained human factuality annotations at the atomic-fact level, and creating such annotations is costly.
statements.label: lack of suitable datasets for non-entity-centric text

problems.explanation: Evaluating hallucinations in long-form, non-entity-centric text is hard because few datasets have fine-grained human annotations at the atomic-fact level, and creating them is expensive. TriQua proposes a flexible fact representation that mixes simple triples with hyperrelational facts to keep context while staying granular. Better datasets would let detectors move beyond short entity-focused snippets.
problems.first_step: Implement the TriQua fact extraction pipeline from "TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation" on a small set of long-form model outputs such as Wikipedia article sections. Compare the resulting hyperrelational facts against standard triple extraction to see if they preserve more context for verification.

problems.title: Faithfulness evaluation remains unresolved

statements.quote: Finally, faithfulness itself remains an open evaluation problem.
statements.label: faithfulness evaluation is unresolved

problems.explanation: Faithfulness, whether a model's output stays grounded in its source, lacks a settled evaluation method, especially for diffusion language models that generate bidirectionally. The paper studies this on table-to-text generation using the ToTTo dataset where highlighted cells make grounding directly testable. A faithfulness metric would let us compare diffusion and autoregressive models on equal footing.
problems.first_step: Download the ToTTo dataset and fine-tune a small masked diffusion model (e.g., MDLM) on a subset of table-to-text pairs. Evaluate faithfulness by checking whether generated tokens align with the highlighted source cells, following the diagnostic setup from "A Diagnostic Study of Faithfulness in Diffusion Language Models for Table-to-Text Generation".

problems.title: Retry recovery rates remain suboptimal for hallucination correction

statements.quote: The primary exhausts its retry budget on 28.7%; intra model retries recover roughly a quarter of those, and cross model fallback recovers a further 16.5% of the remainder.
statements.label: retry recovery rates remain suboptimal

problems.explanation: When a code model hallucinates a package name, retries only recover a fraction of the errors: the primary model exhausts its retry budget on 28.7% of cases, intra-model retries fix about a quarter, and cross-model fallback adds another 16.5% of the remainder. The paper proposes a two-layer detector with a PyPI existence check and a Random Forest classifier. Improving recovery would reduce supply-chain risks from slopsquatting.
problems.first_step: Build the first-layer PyPI existence check from "Names Can Hurt: Spotting Slopsquatting Risks Caused by Package Name Hallucinations in Local Coding LLMs" and run it on a list of package names generated by a local coding LLM. Measure how many hallucinated names the deterministic check catches before any classifier is needed.
